sentences.text: Wendiceratops was a medium-sized ceratopsid that grew to a length of 6 meters and a body mass of 1.5 metric tons.
This dinosaur is distinguished by a broad skull frill and an erect nasal horn, while lacking a vertical spine on the frill.
Its upper jaw contained at least twenty-six tooth positions, and the animal possessed no eye horns.
A broken nasal horn specimen measured 11.5 cm in height and 9 cm in base length, borne on a vertical nasal bone.
The front part of the skull frill was formed by a rectangular squamosal bone, with episquamosals that uniquely curled upwards.
The episquamosals on the front of the frill uniquely curled upwards, a feature not seen in many relatives.
A broken nasal horn specimen measured 11.5 cm in height and 9 cm in base length.
The upper jaw of Wendiceratops contained at least twenty-six tooth positions.
Fossils of Wendiceratops were discovered in 2010 by fossil prospector Wendy Sloboda in the Pinhorn Provincial Reserve in southern Alberta, Canada.
Excavations of these fossils took place between 2011 and 2014.
Paleontologists David Evans and Michael Ryan named and described the genus Wendiceratops pinhornensis in 2015.
The genus name honors the fossil hunter Wendy Sloboda and combines it with the Greek term for 'horned face'.
The holotype specimen, which is the specimen the species is based on, was found in the Oldman Formation.
Wendiceratops shared its habitat in the Oldman Formation with predators like Daspletosaurus and herbivores such as Parasaurolophus.
The discovery of Wendiceratops revealed at least five species of ceratopsids in the lower Oldman Formation, including Albertaceratops, Judiceratops, Medusaceratops, and Avaceratops.
Researchers suggest that the presence of multiple ceratopsid species in the same area was made possible by ecological specializations and high faunal turnover.
Wendiceratops belongs to the family Ceratopsidae.
It is classified in the subfamily Centrosaurinae as a sister species to Sinoceratops.
Researchers view the erect, moderately sized nasal horn of Wendiceratops as a transitional form between low horns of primitive centrosaurines and the high horns of advanced ones.
Wendiceratops lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately 79 to 78 million years ago in the Campanian stage.
Fossils of Wendiceratops have been found in what is now North America.
It is debated whether the long vertical horn of Chasmosaurinae evolved independently in parallel evolution, potentially being the second time such a horn evolved among ceratopsids.
